title: Woodblock printing
summary: Woodblock printing developed in China during the Tang dynasty. By the 9th century, Chinese craftsmen could mass-produce books by carving words and pictures into wooden blocks, inking them and pressing paper onto them. As in Europe centuries later, printing dramatically lowered the price of books, aiding the spread of literacy and boosting drama and popular culture.

uncertainty.note: Block printing emerged during the 7th–8th centuries of the Tang dynasty, achieved widespread commercial and religious book production by the 9th century, and expanded into massive state-sponsored canonical printing during the Song and Goryeo eras.

importance.justification: Woodblock printing was the world's first mechanical technology for text reproduction, sparking an information revolution in literacy, education, and religious practice across East Asia centuries ahead of Western movable type.

reviewer_note: The exact date of invention is unknown. A printed Diamond Sutra of 868 has its own record. The pin at Xi'an, the Tang capital, is a stand-in.
